title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 353
paragraphs: and her temple is laid out thus: except for the entrance, it is completely surrounded by water; for channels come in from the Nile — not joining one another, but each extending as far as the entrance of the temple, one flowing around on one side and the other on the other. Each is a hundred feet broad and shaded over with trees. The gateway rises to a height of ten fathoms and is adorned with figures six cubits high, very striking. This temple stands in the middle of the city, and can be looked down upon from all sides as one walks around; for since the city has been banked up to a height, while the temple has not been moved from where it was originally built, one can look down into it. Around it runs a stone wall with figures carved upon it, and within is a grove of very large trees planted around a great temple-house, inside which stands the image of the goddess. The breadth and length of the temple is a furlong in every direction. Opposite the entrance there is a road paved with stone for about three furlongs, leading through the marketplace toward the east, with a breadth of about four hundred feet. On either side grow trees reaching to the sky, and the road leads to the temple of Hermes. This, then, is how the temple is arranged.
